opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way we approached it started with a common assumption we wanted to test. A lot of people believe that if you ground a model in retrieved documents, it'll be safer. It has the right context, it's less likely to make things up, so surely it's also less likely to produce harmful content. We wanted to check whether that actually holds.

So the setup is fairly direct. You take the same set of models, you take a set of prompts that are designed to elicit unsafe behavior, and you run them in two conditions: once with the model on its own, and once in a RAG configuration where the model is given retrieved documents alongside the query. Then you compare how often the outputs are unsafe, using the same safety classification and the same taxonomy of harms in both settings, so the comparison is apples to apples.

What surprised us, and a lot of people, is that RAG can actually make models *less* safe. Models that are pretty reliably refusing harmful requests in isolation become more willing to answer once you put documents in the context. That happens even when the retrieved documents themselves are benign. It isn't simply a matter of the retriever pulling in something toxic. Something about the combination of a long context and the instruction to use the provided information seems to shift the model's behavior away from its safety training. Those guardrails were mostly tuned in a setting that looks like a short chat turn, not a long grounded prompt.

A few things come out of that for how I think about evaluation more broadly. First, you can't evaluate the safety of a model and assume it transfers to the system. You have to evaluate the system as deployed: the retriever, the prompt template, the documents, the model, all together. Second, safety evaluation needs to be domain-specific. A generic harm taxonomy misses a lot. In financial services, for example, you care about things like giving unauthorized financial advice, leaking confidential information, or misrepresenting facts in ways that have legal implications, and general-purpose guardrails often don't cover those well. And third, the variables you'd think matter don't always matter the way you expect. Things like how many documents you retrieve or how safe those documents are don't map neatly onto output safety. That's another reason you have to measure empirically instead of reasoning your way to "this should be safer."

So the short answer is: treat RAG as a different system with its own risk profile, red-team it in its actual configuration, and don't inherit safety claims from the base model.

r001.rationale: It describes running the same unsafe prompts on models alone and in a RAG configuration, then comparing output safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd push back on a little bit is the framing itself, because there's this very common assumption floating around that if you ground the model in retrieved documents, you've sort of solved the safety problem. The model is just reading from the documents, so what could go wrong? And what we found when we actually looked at it is that this assumption doesn't hold up. RAG changes the safety profile of a system, it doesn't eliminate it, and in some cases it makes things worse in ways that are not intuitive.

So the way I approach it is to start by asking, what's actually different about the setup? In a plain LLM, the unsafe behavior you're worried about comes from the model's parametric knowledge and from whatever the prompt is doing. In a RAG system, you've introduced a whole new input channel. You have documents coming in that the model treats as context, and those documents can be adversarial, they can be outdated, they can be perfectly benign but combine with the question in a way that produces something harmful. So the attack surface is genuinely larger.

And then the thing that surprised us the most is what happens to the model's own refusal behavior. A lot of these models have been trained to decline certain requests, and that training is sensitive to the shape of the input. When you prepend a big chunk of retrieved text, you've changed the distribution. The model is now in a "summarize what's in front of me" mode, and we saw cases where the same question that the model would refuse on its own, it would happily answer once there were documents attached, even when the documents had nothing to do with the harmful part of the request. The retrieved context essentially acted as a distraction that pulled the model out of its safety behavior.

So concretely, the evaluation approach is to hold everything else fixed and vary the retrieval condition. You take the same set of prompts, including ones that probe for unsafe content, and you run them with no retrieval, with relevant retrieval, with irrelevant retrieval, and with deliberately bad retrieval. And you look not just at factuality, which is where most RAG evaluation stops, but at refusal rates, at whether harmful content is generated, and at whether the model is faithful to the documents or is pulling in stuff from its own weights that the documents don't support. That last part matters because the whole promise of RAG is that you can audit the sources, and if the model is silently blending in parametric knowledge, that promise is broken.

The other thing I'd say is that this is very model dependent. We saw different models behave quite differently, and the safety training that works well in the no-retrieval setting doesn't automatically transfer. So I don't think you can evaluate RAG safety once at the architecture level. It has to be done for the specific model, with the specific retriever, on the specific domain you're deploying in. Red teaming the end-to-end system, not just the model in isolation.

r001.rationale: It proposes using the same prompts, including unsafe-content probes, with no retrieval and with different retrieval conditions, then comparing safety outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what we mean by safer, because retrieval changes the failure modes; it doesn’t automatically remove them. Are we concerned about factual errors, revealing sensitive information, or following malicious instructions? Those need different evaluations.

For factuality, I’d compare the same model with and without retrieval on the same questions. But I’d also separate two things: whether the answer is supported by the retrieved documents, and whether those documents are actually correct. A model can faithfully repeat an incorrect source. And a citation by itself isn’t evidence that the cited passage supports the claim.

Then I’d test what happens when retrieval goes wrong. What if the relevant document is missing, two sources contradict each other, or a document contains instructions intended to manipulate the model? Does it acknowledge uncertainty, or confidently produce an answer anyway?

So I wouldn’t reduce this to one aggregate score. I’d want to understand which risks retrieval reduces, which risks it introduces, and how consequential those failures are in the application where we’re deploying it.

r001.rationale: It proposes comparing the same model with and without retrieval on the same questions for factuality, but does not specify comparing responses to unsafe queries.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by asking what we mean by safer, because retrieval can help with some failure modes while introducing others. If we’re concerned about factual errors, giving the model access to relevant evidence can help. But that doesn’t guarantee that it will use the evidence correctly, or that the evidence itself is trustworthy.

So I’d compare the systems on the same questions and look beyond whether the final answer is correct. Did the retriever find the right information? Is the answer actually supported by that information? Do the citations support the claims being made? And when the evidence is missing or contradictory, does the system acknowledge that uncertainty?

I’d also test cases where the retrieved material is misleading or contains instructions trying to manipulate the model. You’ve added another input channel, and that creates another opportunity for things to go wrong.

The important thing is to evaluate the whole system under the conditions where you intend to use it. A higher average accuracy score is useful, but it isn’t enough to establish that a system is safer. You need to understand which failures retrieval reduces, which ones it introduces, and how consequential those failures are.

r001.rationale: The response proposes comparing systems on the same questions, but does not specify that the queries should be unsafe or explicitly compare responses to unsafe queries with and without retrieved context.
